author: anarchy
title: Reflections on a decade of Black Lives Matter UK
content:
Black Lives Matter UK was founded by activists who had worked together on previous deaths in police custody, both in the US and Britain.

In the US, it had started as a love letter to Black people in the aftermath of George Zimmerman’s acquittal – who killed 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012 for the crime of carrying Skittles while Black in a gated community.

In Britain our martyr was Mark Duggan, killed by the Met in 2011. We not only remember the anti-Black propaganda about his criminality, how even some radical leftists argued he needed to die, how the army needed to be brought in to control rioters. We remember the public disregard of his and Black life in general. We live with the reality of State harassment and violence in terms of stop and search, legal sexual assault in terms of strip searches. State racist violence is not only structural, it structures the British economy and State legitimacy.

Today, which is worse than in 2011, almost one in two Black children do not get three meals a day. Ethnically Black African children do better than white British children in GCSEs, but are less likely to get a paid job. All of this motivates us because it is our lived reality.

author: anarchy
title: What’s in a name?
content:
~ Wren Albion (the artist formerly known as Warren Draper) ~

Anarchists have often changed their names. Some have done so fluidly throughout their lives for security reasons. Others, like the author B. Traven, have created pseudonyms which give them a level of anonymity. And others have chosen to adopt a new name which they feel suits the person they have become. Some, like myself, have done all three.

Anyone who has changed their name by deed poll will know that mononyms are not allowed. Official systems are strictly designed for forename/surname combinations. The rise of the surname is inherently linked to the rise of the state. Perhaps the most concise and entertaining history of state-sanctioned naming occurs in the second chapter of Seeing Like a State by the late great James C. Scott. Here Scott describes how, in roughly the 4th Century BC, the Qin Dynasty began to impose patronyms (surnames derived from the male line) on much of the population for the purposes of taxes, forced labour and conscription. The process has been repeated throughout history whenever the centralised state has sought to deepen its hold over the people.

author: Blade
title: Ceuta mass crossing exposes Europe’s deadly border regime
content:
Between 30 and 31 July, an extraordinary movement of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, the Spanish-controlled enclave in North Africa claimed by Morocco. Spain’s Interior Ministry estimated that approximately 50,000 people —most of them young Moroccans—entered by land or sea, while Ceuta’s authorities placed the number closer to 60,000. The Spanish government deployed soldiers and additional police as the existing border and reception systems collapsed.

The death toll remains disputed. Spanish authorities initially reported recovering 57 bodies, then 67, while the Moroccan Association for Human Rights estimated nearly 130 victims.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez attributed the mobilisation principally to misleading social-media posts about a Spanish Supreme Court judgement issued on 8 July. The judgement held that the special border-rejection procedure applying in Ceuta and Melilla could not be used to return people intercepted at sea without an individual legal process. It did not grant migrants a right to remain in Spain, nor did it prevent eventual deportation.

Moroccan human-rights activists confirmed that social-media claims that “the border was open” contributed to the movement. Moroccan security forces were reported to stand aside initially , later to use batons, tear gas, water cannon and warning shots against people attempting to cross.

author: punkacademic
title: The miseducation of Andy Burnham
content:
Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been sounding off about a number of things in his first weeks in office – not least education. Last week, No 10 announced that there was to be a major shake-up in British secondary education , with (in Andy’s words) “new technical education pathways from 14—prestigious routes that will give students the chance to combine the core academic subjects with the skills, technical knowledge and experience they need to get quality, well-paid jobs where they live”.

The problem, as every educator with even a little experience knows, is that it’s all been said before. You can go back as far as the nineteenth century to find employers whinging in the press about the decline of apprenticeships and the need for government to do something, but even in the last four decades we’ve been blessed with everything from BTECs to NVQs to T-levels.

Put bluntly, every initiative to put technical education on the same level as ‘academic’ education has failed. PM Andy intones emphatically that “from today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap”, but saying it, as Prime Minister after Prime Minister has done, doesn’t make it so.

A well-known aside in educational circles which sums up the issue pithily is that for politicians, technical or vocational education is always the answer to the problem… for someone else’s children.

author: anarchy
title: The bane of Murray Bookchin Thought
content:
Murray Bookchin is rightly remembered for many things. He was a self-declared anarchist for a little more than three decades; according to the hagiography written by his long-term partner he became one in the late 1950s after moving away from the Stalinism of his youth, but he didn’t become known as one under his own name until the late 60s. Plenty of other anarchists found his analyses and positions to be lacking – he abandoned class struggle in the early 70s, tried to make common cause with the nascent right-wing “anarchists” of the Libertarian Party around the same time (even speaking at one of their conventions!), offered extremely uncritical support for the Sandinistas (because their red and black flag symbolised their adherence to anarcho-syndicalism – I’m not kidding), maintained a stubbornly inexplicable adherence to a Marxoid Hegelianism, and had a love-hate relationship with electoral politics by co-founding a local chapter of the Green Party.

By the mid-1980s, many of his critics had accused him of veering away from the recognisable principles of anarchism, an allegation he studiously ignored. author: anarchy
title: Murray Bookchin’s liberatory legacy
content:
Murray Bookchin was a person that devoted his life to the development of Social Ecology and Communalism as theoretical tools of a comprehensive social project for the challenges that both humanity and nature face. Through tireless teaching, speaking, organising, and writing, Bookchin presented a humanist vision of ecology based on community, direct democracy, and the better promises of the Enlightenment, showing how we could transform our society into one that is free and egalitarian.

Bookchin was not interested in creating a new political dogma or metaphysical ideology, which to elevate him to an “armchair” intellectual status, while providing his audience with post-modern fancy word-salads. No, he was not interested in this and was not afraid to engage in fierce political debates with other thinkers and political tendencies. Bookchin did not hesitate to criticise the postmodernist nihilist politics of renowned philosophers of past and present like Nietzsche, Heidegger, Foucault, Derrida, Lyotard, Deleuze, and Baudrillard. He was also highly critical of political movements like anarcho-syndicalism and Marxism . Bookchin recognised their historic importance, but couldn’t overlook their role today—an attempt to fall back, in times of a terribly fragmented reality, onto obsolete, even archaic ideologies in a search for a sense of continuity and security. author: anarchy
title: Remembering Murray Bookchin
content:
Murray Bookchin was one of the most relevant voices in the ecological debate all throughout the second half of the 20th century, combining deep philosophical, anthropological and historical knowledge on the one hand, and some brilliant political insights on the other hand. His intellectual biography is a complex one, merging intellectual and militant engagement, and ranging from syndicalism to Trotskyism, and later anarchism. Importantly, he developed the concept of social ecology, for which he is best known. The many polemics in which he was involved made him a controversial figure in the anarchist movement, but the relevance and originality of his contributions are out of question.

From Marxism via anarchism to communalism

Murray Bookchin’s political engagement starts at a very young age, under the influence of the socialist ideas that his grandmother taught him since he was a kid. As a 15-year-old, he tried to enlist for the Spanish Civil War and got refused because of his young age. As a young factory worker, he was engaged in syndicalist struggles, and broke with his Stalinist political affiliation before turning 20. He embraced Trotskyist ideas and joined the Socialist Workers Party and the United Electrical Workers while working at General Motors. author: anarchy
title: Why we disrupted the International AIDS Conference
content:
On Monday, I was among the protesters who stormed the opening ceremony of the 26th International AIDS Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brasil, the largest scientific conference on HIV in the world. I was there alongside comrades from organisations including ACT UP, HealthGap, Médecins Sans Frontières, HIV i-base, and the Health Justice Initiative. We took the microphones, raising our voices against the greed of pharmaceutical companies, and the complicity of governments who have slashed their humanitarian aid, severely affecting efforts to combat diseases such as HIV.

Our protests had begun before the official opening. After gathering at 7 AM, we interrupted a presentation by Jeff Graham, acting US Global AIDS Coordinator and the man responsible for the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which the Trump administration gutted in early 2025. We raised placards reading “Stop the Blackmail. Stop the Lies. Release PEPFAR Funds. Follow the Science” and “Trump’s Cuts Kill People with AIDS. Restore PEPFAR Now”. We chanted “You lie, we die,” while South African campaigners added a single word: “Murderer.”

author: anarchy
title: BASH BACK shatters Ann Widdecombe smear campaign
content:
Transgender direct action group BASH BACK has made a devastating rebuttal to an article in The Times , in which Lord Walney suggests Britain should move to proscribe groups engaging in “systematic criminal disruption”. Lord Walney is former right-wing Labour MP John Woodcock, who quit Parliament following sexual harassment allegations . While serving as the government’s “independent adviser on political violence and disruption”, he was an active lobbyist for fossil fuel interests and the arms industry.

The article was preceded by an extensive news report which repeats quotes from the article, padded with reminders of previous scaremongering coverage of BASH BACK in The Times. In their statement, included below, activists from BASH BACK argue that the “paranoia from the authoritarian right stems from a need to protect property, ideology, and profit”. The group states it stands behind all its previous actions and reiterates its commitment to non-violence.

In the paywalled article, Woodcock castigates BASH BACK for not removing the image of a hammer breaking glass from its website after Ann Widdecombe was murdered with a hammer on 8 June. Walney is careful not to allege any direct connection, and makes no reference to Widdecombe’s infamous crusade against LGBTQI+ rights . author: anarchy
title: German syndicalists in revolutionary Spain
content:
Summer 1936 in Germany: Month after month, year after year, the oppressive swelter of impending hopelessness gripped the comrades. For over three years, fascism had been stifling life in the country. Almost all anarcho-syndicalist functionaries had suffered house searches, confiscations, arrests, imprisonment in concentration camps, and torture. Some did not survive. Secretly, relatives and comrades organised aid for the prisoners and their families, printed and distributed illegal newspapers, and created routes of escape. By the end of the year, the Nazi state had dismantled almost all anarcho-syndicalist resistance networks.

But suddenly, exactly what many had given up on happening, happened. Fascism was beatable! And not through elections, governments, or military liberation from the outside. What anarcho-syndicalists all over the world had longed for for decades was a reality: social revolution in Spain, and perhaps soon throughout the world!

To mark the 90th anniversary of the Spanish Revolution, I unearthed many German-language eyewitness accounts and compiled them in the book Great, Beautiful, Unforgettable Days (AV Publishing, in German). These original “Voices from the Spanish Revolution” form a compelling and instructive history of German anarcho-syndicalists as part of the struggles there for a free society based on liberty, equality, and mutual aid.

title: Club Esportiu Júpiter and the Barcelona anarchists
content:
Little remains of historic Poblenou. This working-class neighbourhood has been transformed by urban renewal. In the collective work Barcelona Rebelde , published in 2003, Agustín Guillamón revisited a chapter in the history of the neighbourhood and its football club: Club Esportiu Júpiter, which distinguished itself by supporting the anarchist workers who took up arms against the military uprising launched by Franco.

At the beginning of the 20th century, it wasn’t uncommon for a football club to be born at a corner of a table in the back of a bar. This was the case with Club Esportiu Júpiter, founded on May 12, 1909, by the Mauchan brothers, British workers at the Fabra & Coats factory in the heart of the Poblenou district, the industrial heart of Catalonia. David, one of the three Mauchan brothers, had previously played for El Escosès, the Scottish diaspora club. CE Júpiter is a team that blends Catalan and British players.
